title: Be the Liquidity Provider
objectives: Deposit a matched pair into a pool and understand exactly what you get back
Follow trading fees from the swap into the vault and into your LP token
Read the minting math that protects early depositors
Know what an exit actually returns — it is never your original deposit

steps.title: How Liquidity Providers Earn Fees
steps.body:
AMMs only work because ordinary people put tokens into the shared pot. Those people are liquidity providers, and what they do is simpler than it sounds.

You deposit equal values of both tokens — $100 of SOL and $100 of fUSDC. The contract measures your deposit against everything already in the pool, then mints you <Term id="lp_token">LP tokens</Term>. Those tokens are the receipt: they encode exactly what percentage of the pool you now own.

Equal values matter because a pool is a balanced scale. Deposit lopsided and the scale tips, which is free money for the next arbitrage bot. By depositing 50/50 you hand the <Term id="amm">formula</Term> the two ingredients in the proportion it already expects.

Follow your $200 through the machine:

1. You send $100 SOL and $100 fUSDC to the pool contract.
2. The contract works out what fraction of the <Term id="liquidity_pool">liquidity pool</Term> that is.
3. It mints LP tokens proving your claim.
4. Traders swap against the pot 24/7 while your share sits there.

You have not bought anything and you have not lent to anybody. You bought a slice of a live marketplace, and that slice earns a cut of every trade that happens inside it.

steps.title: Trading Fees: The LP Yield Engine
steps.body:
Every <Term id="swap">swap</Term> through the pool pays a fee, typically 0.3%. That fee does not go to a bank, a company, or a founder wallet. It goes straight back into the pool's reserves.

Walk one trade through:

- A trader swaps $1,000 of fUSDC into SOL.
- The pool keeps $3 and adds it to the reserves.
- At that instant your LP tokens can be redeemed for a slightly larger slice of tokens than a moment before.

Fees never appear as a separate payment. They quietly grow what each LP unit redeems for. That is the whole engine.

The trade-off is obvious once you say it out loud: more volume means more fees landing in the vault, so where you park liquidity matters as much as how much you deposit.

When you want out, you burn the LP tokens. The contract returns your proportional slice of the current reserves — your capital plus every fee collected while you were inside.

One warning before that sounds too easy. Fees are on your side; violent price swings are not. Read <Term id="impermanent_loss">impermanent loss</Term> before you go all-in on a pool.

steps.title: Under the Hood: LP Token Minting Math
steps.body:
On the very first deposit the contract mints `sqrt(amountA × amountB)` LP tokens, minus a tiny amount — around 1,000 units — that is locked forever.

Every deposit after that mints proportionally:

`LP tokens = min(amountA / reserveA, amountB / reserveB) × totalLPSupply`

Reading that like an LP:

- The square root anchors the first LP unit to the pool's geometry rather than to any currency, so the opening price cannot be gamed.
- The `min(...)` protects the people already inside. Deposit lopsided and you only get credit for the side that matches the pool's ratio.
- The locked 1,000 units are a floor. Without them someone could drain the pool to near-zero and attack the accounting. With them the last withdrawal is never worth taking.

On the way out the contract simply burns your tokens and hands back your share of the live reserves. Fees collected along the way are already baked into those reserves, so there is no separate payout to claim.

questions.prompt: You make your very first deposit of $100 SOL + $100 fUSDC into a pool. What does the smart contract give you back?
options: Nothing - you only see percentage points in the app dashboard, the contract keeps no record of you
A loan worth 100% of your deposit that you must repay to the pool within 30 days
An LP token receipt that represents your proportional ownership share of the entire pool
A coupon giving you 0.3% off your personal swap fees in that pool forever
questions.explainRight: LP tokens are a redeemable claim on a fraction of the pool, minted by the contract. When you burn them later, the contract honours that fraction using whatever the pool holds at that moment.
questions.explainWrong: It is not a loan — you owe nothing back — and it is not a discount coupon. A real pool always mints a real receipt. If an app shows you 'percentage points' with no token behind them, treat that as a red flag.

questions.prompt: A trader swaps $1,000 through a pool with a 0.3% fee. Where does that $3 fee actually go?
options: It is destroyed, so the pool slowly loses value and every LP position shrinks over time
It is deposited back into the pool's vaults, making each LP token redeemable for slightly more underlying tokens
It is split 50/50 between the trader and the most recent depositor
It is sent to a centralized protocol administrator as operating revenue
questions.explainRight: The $3 never leaves the pool. It is added to the reserves backing every LP token, so each token redeems for a little more than it did a moment before. More volume means the vault grows faster.
questions.explainWrong: Fees do not shrink the pool and do not leave it. In a standard AMM the cut goes back into the reserves, which is exactly why LP tokens gain redemption value over time.

questions.prompt: Two LPs deposited the same dollar value a month ago. LP A's pool has had 10x more swap volume than LP B's pool. Which statement is the most accurate?
options: LP A's tokens are redeemable for more underlying tokens, because more swap fees accumulated in that pool's reserves
They earn identical returns because all AMM LP tokens pay a fixed annual dividend set at deployment
LP A's pool automatically printed more LP tokens to compensate for the extra traffic
The volume difference only matters if the pool price changes by more than 5% in a single day
questions.explainRight: Fees land in the vault of the pool that actually saw the trades. Ten times the volume means ten times the fee cuts in LP A's reserves, so each LP token there redeems for more.
questions.explainWrong: There is no fixed dividend paid regardless of usage. Fee income comes from real trading, and the busier pool accumulates more of it. No extra LP tokens are printed as a thank-you for traffic.

questions.prompt: Why does the smart contract permanently lock about 1,000 LP tokens from the very first deposit?
options: It pays validator priority fees so the pool can execute swaps faster under congestion
It funds future security audits so the pool stays audited forever without extra cost
It creates intentional deflation that makes every LP token slightly more scarce over time
It acts as 'minimum liquidity' so draining the pool completely becomes economically unattractive
questions.explainRight: A pool that could be drained to near-zero is attackable: deposit a little, scoop out the last sliver, leave the accounting broken. Locking a floor of ~1,000 units makes that last withdrawal worthless to attempt.
questions.explainWrong: It is not for gas, audits, or deflation. The locked units are a security floor written into the maths, so nobody can economically extract the reserves down to zero.

questions.prompt: You hold 150 of the 15,000 total LP tokens in a pool. The pool accumulates $4,500 of trading fees. Roughly how much of those fees is yours?
questions.explainRight: 150 out of 15,000 is exactly 1%, so 1% of $4,500 is $45. Your slice is always your tokens divided by the total supply — nothing more complicated than that.
questions.explainWrong: Work the fraction first: 150 / 15,000 = 1%. One percent of $4,500 is $45. This is why understanding 'your tokens over total supply' matters more than memorising numbers off a dashboard.

questions.prompt: You burn all your LP tokens back to the pool to exit. Which of the following best describes what the contract actually returns to you?
options: Exactly your original deposit in the exact same amounts and coins you put in
A USD-denominated payout equal to what your deposit was worth on day one
Your proportional slice of the pool's CURRENT reserves - original capital plus earned fees, minus whatever the price ratio shifted since you deposited
A fresh set of LP tokens you can immediately re-deposit, so you never really leave the pool
questions.explainRight: Burning returns your share of the reserves as they are now, not as they were when you entered. Fees raised the total; the rebalancing changed the mix. You leave with a different composition than you arrived with.
questions.explainWrong: An LP exit is not a refund of the original deposit. The contract pays out the current contents of the pool, in whatever ratio the trades have moved it to. There is no USD promise and no time capsule.

questions.prompt: A trader swaps 5 SOL into the pool on its fUSDC side, paying the full 0.3% fee. Right afterward, you withdraw your LP share. What is the most accurate description of the pool state you are exiting?
options: It holds more SOL, less fUSDC, and the 5 SOL PLUS the fee have been added to its reserves - your exit value reflects both the rebalanced ratio and the accrued fee
It holds exactly the same reserves as before, because a swap is a zero-sum exchange that leaves total quantity untouched
The trader's 5 SOL stays locked in escrow for 30 days, so only the fee is added to the pool now
Your LP share permanently shrinks by 0.3% for every swap that happens while you are inside
questions.explainRight: A swap changes the pool twice: it adds the input token with its fee, and it drains the output token. You exit a vault holding more total value and a different ratio than the day you walked in.
questions.explainWrong: Swaps are not zero-sum for the pool. Each one injects the input plus the fee and removes output, so reserves grow and tilt. Your LP share does not shrink by 0.3% per trade — what changes is the contents you redeem from.
